Mr. Chairman, there is only one matter I should like to raise this evening one that was discussed at length this afternoon. I am speaking of the matter of parole and the activities of the National Parole Board. I am sure we all realize the task that is faced by the National Parole Board in making decisions with respect to the cases brought before them. Some of these cases are probably more difficult than others, but I suppose that even the easiest case is not too easy to deal with. They all have their own particular problems and situations, and we can sympathize with the National Parole Board in the work it is attempting to do. There is considerable talk these days about "going soft" on criminals. Other people think society is hard on criminals. However, Mr. Chairman, I shall not discuss that particular aspect of the matter at this time.

I wish to bring just one matter to the attention of the minister. I believe this case emphasizes the importance of considering the human element in these problems and perhaps giving the benefit of the doubt in certain cases. I have here a brief that has been built up through correspondence. It concerns the work of the Mennonite central committee, an organization that is doing very fine work in various fields of activity. This organization is working in my own constituency and has established what is called a halfway house project. The objective of the project is to rehabilitate those who have broken the law; to provide means whereby they can be rehabilitated and assist in their own rehabilitation.
The case to which I refer concerns one of the Sons of Freedom who was incarcerated in Mountain Prison at Agassiz, British Columbia. I understand that about five brothers were sentenced. The youngest of them was paroled some time ago. The Mennonite central committee, in an endeavour to assist, contacted the family of one of these men and persuaded them to leave the camp which had been established just outside Mountain Prison. The committee persuaded the family to live in the community of Yarrow, British Columbia, in a home that had been provided by them. The family was looked after by the Mennonite central committee.
Representations were then made to try to effect the parole of the husband and father of this family. For some reason or other the parole board decided against the application. This took place back in August of last year, and I understand this man is still incarcerated. I believe this is a case that should receive very careful and special consideration. Here is an organization that on its own initiative went ahead and provided facilities for this family. They felt it would help to get the family away from the main body of this particular group, the Sons of Freedom, so they persuaded them to live elsewhere and endeavoured to reunite the family and provide the man with a job and proper supervision. They were prepared to assist in his rehabilitation. As I have pointed out, the National Parole Board ruled against the application and apparently it will not be renewed until 1968.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because I believe organizations such as this ought to be encouraged in this type of work. I believe also that if we can bring these families together, away from the ordinary environment in which they find themselves, it will assist tremendously in rehabilitation. I
June 26, 1967	COMMONS
will present the minister with the name of this person and family and will outline the brief to him. I trust he will give this matter careful consideration and see whether anything can be done to assist them.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to ask a question rather than to make anything in the nature of a speech. I should like to ask the minister to consider, if he would, the reform of the bail system of Canada as proposed in my own bill, No. C-4, as well as several other places.
This bill is quite in line with legislation established last year in the United States. In brief, to quote from the explanatory notes of the proposed legislation, it would reform the present bail system in Canada as our American friends did about 12 months ago. It would effect this reform in the following way. The bill would assure that all persons, regardless of their financial status, should not needlessly be detained pending their appearance to answer charges under acts of the parliament of Canada, when detention served neither the ends of justice nor the public interest.
The measure I propose, and which I would ask the minister to consider, would permit poor people awaiting trial to be released without bond and would thus eliminate the arbitrary cruelty in the present bail system. It would permit them to be released without bond, in the absence of cash, having in mind certain other precautionary and amending steps. The present bail system requires that there shall be cash in all cases before bail can be granted.
The system of release without bail which would be established by the bill I propose would be limited to instances where the offence is not punishable by death or life imprisonment and in which the judge deems the defendent trustworthy. I would ask the minister to take into consideration the reform of the bail system in line with the general terms and principles of my proposal.

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister on the presentation of his estimates. I have found him to be deeply interested in the problems that he faces in his department, and I have also found him most co-operative in dealing with questions that are raised by constituents and presented to him. I believe the evidence presented by hon. members today in the representations that have been made to the minister indicates the feeling amongst all
DEBATES	1965
Supply-Solicitor General members of the house, that they have a sympathetic ear to which to present vigorously the problems of people who come under the jurisdiction of the legal system. Hon. members know that tbe minister will give his best consideration to analysing their suggestions and incorporating those which seem to offer better hope in the future.
The ministers' co-operation in regard to settling the feelings of despair, perhaps, in regard to the changing picture of the R.C.M.P. establishment, especially in my constituency, was deeply appreciated. I know that the visit he undertook during the course of a busy schedule, and on rather short notice at the time, was well worth while and he made a good contribution to better understanding. For that we owe the minister our deepest thanks.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I have listened to all the representations made today about those who run afoul of the law and are incarcerated. I shall not repeat the representations that have been made but I should like to bring to the attention of the minister one matter that bothers me. I confess that I am no expert in this field and perhaps do not know all the details I should know when bringing the matter to the minister's attention. I know it costs a great deal of money to keep a person in an institution, and sometimes when I see the small budgets of the John Howard and Elizabeth Fry societies as well as those of other agencies engaged in the work of fulfilling what seems to me to be a very pertinent and desirable service I wonder whether we should not look more deeply into the objective of rehabilitation and treatment of the inmates. It seems to me that the people who come out of prisons are virtually put out on the street and not a great deal is done to help them. Prisoners on parole often fall back into crime again. There is no doubt that often there is a great deal of co-operation being given by the families concerned to assist the parole board and other authorities. Paroles are being granted to prisoners so as to give them a fair chance to remain out of trouble and to fit them into society. There are also prisoners who serve their sentences without being paroled. It seems to me that very little is provided for them.
We all know the prejudice against anybody who has been in trouble with the law and who has served time. It is difficult for him to obtain employment and to rehabilitate himself. It costs us $3,000 or $4,000 a year to keep them in security and to try to instil in them a
June 26. 1967

Supply-Solicitor General desire to fit into society. It seems to me ridiculous that after having expended so much money on these people no further help is provided them.
Perhaps the minister could tell me where in the estimates grants to the John Howard or Elizabeth Fry societies are provided and on what basis these grants are established. Are they established on the basis of the previous year's case load and the contributions that have been made? We all know that these societies are continually upgrading their staff. They are obtaining professional staff and, as is emphasized in their reports, their caseloads demand an increased number of professional staff. Yet sufficient funds are not provided for them. I noticed in some reports that municipalities provide amounts ranging from $25 to $100 for that purpose, but on what basis is this done? I wonder if the minister could indicate to the house what part in his view these societies are expected to play. I should like him to explain to us on what basis they are provided with part of their budget to enable them to play their part efficiently and well.
That is the only point I wish to bring up, in addition to the various representations that have been made to the minister. I am quite impressed by the recommendation that first offenders in a great many cases should not be incarcerated. I agree that Parkinson's law seems to work in all stratas of society and if we build institutions we will fill them. However, if we develop a more enlightened attitude and help former prisoners to play their part in the community, and help them to stay out of trouble, we will not need to worry about building so many institutions and thus will achieve a net gain both in money saved and in a decrease in crime.
I know that the changing times have brought about an increase in the R.C.M.P. establishment. I do not need to relate again the historic significance of the force in my area and what it means to the community. I believe it is in fact a very desirable and suitable location for the work that is done there and for the courses that are being followed. I notice the minister in his opening statement on June 6 referred to an increase in the establishment from 9,500 to 11,000. This of course means that more trainees are being admitted and more work is being done in this regard.
He also referred to a new Canadian police college, and I wonder whether he has in mind a new building or a whole new establishment. If so, will this establishment be operated as a primary training centre at Regina? I know

that police courses have been held there for many years. I have been in contact with these people and I know that police forces from many countries have been drawn to that institution. I am acquainted with their methods of training, and if it is the minister's intention to enlarge the establishment, I am wholly in favour of it. In view of the mounting expenditures I do not expect a great deal of money to be provided in addition to the amounts already outlined, but I do hope priorities will be established so as to allow the opening of this college at Regina, and the continued training of the police force in its new sophisticated form so as to meet the necessary requirements.
The other matter to which I wish to refer concerns the museum at the Regina establishment. I think the minister has seen it and must realize that the quarters are not adequate. It has been a great tourist attraction. I believe the time has come when a permanent curator should be appointed and new quarters provided for the museum. This would provide considerable space for other activities of the force. I hope this matter will be given the necessary priority, and that the minister will be able to tell us that provision will be made for the museum and its exhibits in Regina city, and that priority is given for the establishment of new quarters and perhaps the appointment of a permanent curator so that this very desirable operation can be continued in the future.
Once again I want to thank the minister for his co-operation. I will listen with interest to the answers he will give to the numerous questions and representations which have been made during this debate.

Mr. Chairman, I also would like first of all to express appreciation to the Solicitor General not only for the sympathetic way in which he has listened to the many representations which were made to him, but also for the interest he has shown for the new developments in Canadian penology and his desire to make still further improvements in this regard. This is why I should like to make this evening a special plea on behalf of an institution which is located in my riding and which is doing work for the entire province. I am referring to the Vancouver Halfway House, about which both the hon. member for Vancouver East and I have spoken. A little time ago we went to see the minister with regard to this project, and were very sympathetically received. The people at Halfway
June 26. 1967

House were hoping at that time that the minister would pay them a visit. My purpose tonight is to refresh the minister's memory a little bit and add some new facts to the story. I have been speaking with some of the people out there-in fact I just returned about an hour or so ago-and they are most anxious to have the minister look into this matter without delay.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
This is one of those experimental projects, of which we have had quite a few in Vancouver and some of which have worked out exceedingly well. I am thinking of one which was started under the aegis of the father of the hon. member for Vancouver East, when he was a member of the legislature. At that time he conceived the idea that a good many women who were being released from mental institutions needed a place to go in order to get re-established in ordinary life. A co-operative boarding house was established where they could stay until they found jobs for themselves and became acclimatized to the outside world. This project was frowned upon by a number of people in its initial stages, but eventually became such a success that the provincial government took it over.
This Halfway House in Vancouver is in somewhat the same category. It was started in 1965 by a number of people who were convinced that there was a need for a place for people who wanted to get rid of the drug habit, a place where they could be surrounded by a home atmosphere and where they could deal with this habit under carefully controlled conditions until they were rehabilitated. These people were encouraged to get a job as soon as they were able, preferably outside Vancouver since drugs were more easily available there. Vancouver of course is one of the worst drug centres in Canada.
Since the Vancouver Halfway House was begun in 1965, almost two years ago, over 400 persons have been in residence. A large percentage of these people have at some time been charged with an offence connected with drugs. Some of them of course have come straight from Oakalla, or the penitentiary, but no one is turned away, provided they indicate a desire to attempt withdrawal from the drug habit. In addition, some of these people are parolees. It is significant that the parole board, recognizing the value of the house, has taken a favourable view of it in relation to parolees.
I visited Halfway House at Christmastime. It is located just two blocks from where I live,
Supply-Solicitor General and I shall be going back regularly during the time the house is in recess this summer, if we get sufficient time off. I was most interested in what I saw there that afternoon. The people who are doing the work at the house are themselves in a more advanced stage of withdrawal from the drug. The directors are citizens of Vancouver from different walks of life. I believe there is a United Church minister on the board, as well as a former member of the legislature. A number of the directors have been in business, and it is rather significant that there are four registered physicians on the board of directors. This fact is of importance with regard to the prescribed doses of methadon, which is a withdrawal drug.
The directors have written a letter to the Minister of National Health and Welfare in which they state they are aware that the police forces, provincial and mounted police, have had many reservations about Halfway House. However, the attitude of these forces is changing for the better at the present time, and the directors are seeking an interview with the top officers of both police departments.
This work has been conducted, as well as it is possible to do, in one of the old houses in Vancouver. It is a very old, ramshackle house of the shingle type. These people are doing well, considering the limitations placed upon them by the place in which they work. It is very interesting to note that within the last two weeks seven people from Halfway House have found employment in various parts of the province, two of them in Vancouver and the other five outside the city. When I was there at Christmas I found they kept a very careful record of two things. They keep a careful record of the people who come in, the jobs they get and where they are located. They also keep a record of where every single tablet of that methadon drug goes. There is nothing to the objection raised by some people that this house is a place where methadon can be passed on to other people. They keep track of every single tablet, and I am assured it is used right in the house under the supervision of the prescribing doctors.
As proof of the fact this place is doing good work, I can cite the fact it is now the recipient of a grant of $1,000 per month from the city of Vancouver and the provincial government. The officials of Halfway House have to supply to the city of Vancouver and the provincial government a monthly medical statement and a monthly financial statement. Both the provincial government and the city therefore are
June 26/ 1967

Supply-Solicitor General satisfied this is a responsible organization which is doing a commendable job. Of course this organization is saving the city and provincial government a great deal of money by getting jobs for people who are in quite hopeless condition upon arrival there.
The point is that the board of directors need another establishment. They do not want to do away with the one they have now, because it is essential, but they want another place where they can put people who have partly withdrawn from the habit, in order to keep them for a longer time and keep them away from those in the early withdrawal stage. I can well understand the reason for this because the afternoon I was there at Christmastime someone who had been there for less than 24 hours had a complete seizure and was taken out to be dealt with by the people in the house. This crisis resulted from the beginning of withdrawal from drugs. I also saw the effect of this disaster on the inmates of the house. As a matter of fact, I felt it was having a very bad effect on the others who were a bit farther along with the withdrawal treatment. Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief; I have just a few points I want to bring to the attention of the minister.
My first point is with respect to preliminary inquiries. I should like to recommend to the minister that he give serious consideration to amending the Criminal Code to provide that all preliminary inquiries be held in camera. The purpose of the proposal is to protect the reputations of innocent people against whom charges are brought, but are dismissed at the preliminary inquiry.
There have been many cases of this in Montreal during recent years. I can think of several, but I am not going to mention the names of the people involved because they have had enough bad publicity as it is. These people have had charges brought against them, and the judge at the preliminary inquiry has dismissed the charges as being without any foundation whatever. However, as a result of the charges that were brought and the widespread publicity which accompanied them, the reputations of these people have been ruined to the extent that many of them cannot obtain jobs or cannot even continue to live in the districts in the city in which they have lived for years.
If at the preliminary inquiry there is found to be sufficient evidence to proceed to trial, then it is understandable that the trial should be held in public. However, I think that some serious consideration should be given to holding preliminary inquiries in camera. I believe that the bar association has endorsed this proposal, so it is not a proposal that has been put forward without due consideration being given to it.
I have two other brief points. I am not too sure whether they come under the jurisdiction of the minister but I shall mention them anyway. One is with respect to compensation for
June 26. 1967	COMMONS
the victims of crime. There is before the house a private member's motion on this subject. When it came before the house recently I spoke in favour of it. The matter was also brought up during the debate on capital punishment. Compensation boards of this sort have already been introduced in New Zealand and Great Britain, and I think they are very necessary.
Take for example crimes of violence, where the accused are convicted and sentenced to prison. There is no recourse to compensation for the persons who are the victims of such crimes. Since it is the duty of the state to protect the public against crime, if the state fails in its duty and a crime is committed then there should be some compensation to the victim. Often persons suffer from assault, rape or different types of injury, either to their persons or to their property, but there is no way to repair this damage. I think we should closely follow the experience in Great Britain and New Zealand and look into this question.
My last point relates to costs incurred by persons accused of crime. Again I think that if a person is accused of a crime but after preliminary inquiry the charge against him is dismissed, some reimbursement should be made of the costs incurred by the defendent, who must engage a lawyer and go to a lot of trouble to defend himself against a criminal suit. I cannot see why the costs should not be reimbursed, in the same way as when a per son successfully wins a suit in a civil case.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I put these three points to the minister. The first is that we should consider holding preliminary inquiries in camera; the second is that there should be some means to compensate the victims of crime, especially victims of crimes of violence; and third, we should consider some method by which the costs of an accused person who is found not guilty at preliminary inquiry should be reimbursed to him.

This is pioneer legislation for Canada. I wish to say a word or two about law enforcement officers. Unquestionably our law enforcement officers today have an increasingly difficult role. We live in an entirely different world from the one that many of us were brought up in. Many of the complications in our society today we were unaware of in our youth, or we thought that they did not exist. I must say at this point that I agree with the remarks of the leader of the official opposition when he referred to the histories of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. To some extent, I also agree with his contentions, that the public's image of the force and its appreciation of the force has declined owing to the requirement that the force spend a good deal of time in dealing with traffic violations. I think there is some validity to that contention. Those duties have affected the image of the force -particularly its image with younger people, though other persons have also expressed that view.
On a number of occasions in recent years I have noticed the growing inhumanity nf man to man. Not long ago I was crossing an intersection in this city when a bus driver was driving through on the light. He had the right of way. No passenger was in the bus. Four men under the influence of liquor drove in front of this bus, and the bus driver dented their car in and pushed it along the tracks.
[Mr. Herridge.l

Possibly a dozen people who were on the corners at the time of the accident all disappeared. I then heard the men getting out of the car and saying that they were going to charge the bus driver with crossing against the light. I heard this going on, went over to the group and listened to the conversation for a minute or so. The men said they would lay a charge as soon as they could find a policeman. I then said to the bus driver: "If you want a defence, here is my card. I am willing to go into court and say what actually happened, because I saw it." As soon as I said that, the men got back into their car and drove off.
Members of the R.C.M.P., as all of us are, are human-Mr. Chairman, I am not actually a saint, although many people think I am- and therefore they make mistakes. From my experience, any complaints that I made to a senior officer or detachment head were immediately investigated, and where action was required to remedy the complaint, action was taken.
Less than six weeks ago a man dropped dead outside the entrance to the east block. Everybody hurried by. The man who was with him when he dropped appealed to those around him for help to carry the afflicted man. It was not known then that the man was dead. An appeal was made to help carry the man to the Chateau Laurier. In the end the friend had to leave the afflicted man lying on the sidewalk, go down to the Chateau and get some employees to help carry the man down to the Chateau. A situation of this kind is incredible; yet that sort of thing happens in the society in which we live. It would never have happened a few years ago. These incidents show the influences that are brought to bear on our young people. To some extent we are all guilty of the circumstances under which we live today.
In that connection may I conclude by reading a paragraph or two from an article headed "Let's Face It". It is a commentary by Barbara W. Tuchman, and has a further heading "The Missing Element-Moral Courage":
Of all the ills that our poor criticized, analysed, soeiologized society is heir to, the focal one, it seems to me, from which so much of our uneasiness and confusion derive, is the absence of standards. We are too unsure of ourselves to assert them, to stick by them, if necessary in the case of persons who occupy positions of authority, to impose them. We seem to be afflicted by a widespread and eroding reluctance to take any stand on any values, moral, behavioral or esthetic.
Everyone is afraid to call anything wrong, or vulgar, or fraudulent, or just bad taste or bad manners.
June 26, 1967

Then the article goes on:
Since then, the human species has been busy overbreeding, polluting the air, destroying the balance of nature and bungling in a variety of directions so it is no wonder that we have begun to doubt man's capacity for good judgment. It is hardly surprising that the self-confidence of the nineteenth century and its belief in human progress have been dissipated. "Every great civilization," said Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare John Gardner last year, "has been characterized by confidence in itself." At mid-twentieth century, the supply is low. As a result we tend to shy away from all judgments. We hesitate to label anything wrong and therefore hesitate to require the individual to bear moral responsibility for his acts ...
What it requires is courage-just a little, not very much-the courage to be independent and stand up for the standard of values one believes in. That kind of courage is the quality most conspicuously missing, I think, in current life.
I agree with many of the opinions held by the writer of the article.
In conclusion I wish to say this: Every one of us, in my opinion, has some personal responsibility for the maintenance of value standards, if democracy is to be maintained and improved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the original concept of that movement which is called the Estates General of French Canada is quite commendable. It is a very pleasant idea to take stock of the French fact in the country, to make an analysis, as comprehensive as possible, of the position of the French speaking Canadians in the North American context, and to explore all the avenues likely to insure a maximum spread to that large and great community which gets
June 26. 1967

from the French language an essential dynamism.
The word therapy, many a time, proved to be the most detrimental pitfall for the interests of French-speaking Canadians. Excessive verbalism, useless logomachy have too many times held back worthwhile energies which could have been much more useful somewhere else. An all new Quebec lexicon, during the last few years, displayed the following words:	Associated States, independentism,
particular status, co-operative federalism, and so on-a new terminology which does not fail to kindle constitutional discussions which keep Quebec in a ferment.
The Estates General have taken upon themselves the mission of preventing a sterile selfsatisfaction in flatulent speeches so as to promote a deeper awareness of our national reality. They want to establish a common denominator. The protagonists of this initiative surely deserve the most respectful regard, and I would like to know to what extent the government is ready to give favourable consideration to this initiative.
Evidently, Mr. Speaker, I am conscious, for having taken part personally in its work, of that fact that the Estates General have run the risk of infiltration, but I think that since the elections of last April, a measure of success has been achieved in getting members whose objectivity has been proven.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government-and I am talking about the federal government as a whole, not on a partisan basis-has failed far too long to act like the government of all Canadians, and that explains to some extent the feeling of frustration which the provincial authorities express quite frequently.
I think that the federal authorities should show themselves as open-minded as possible to the aspirations of French Canada while, at the same time, seeing to it that a social order which benefits the Canadian community as a whole is respected.
Under the leadership of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), a new climate has been created, our people are allowed to participate more actively in the administration of the country and the bicultural character of Canada is stressed more.
Federal authorities have a moral responsibility to clear up the political atmosphere and to stop this ideological trend that tends more and more to convince the younger generation of Quebeckers that to be in Ottawa is to render a disservice to French-speaking Canada.

There is no more obvious error than that, and I am happy to note to what extent the present Prime Minister has co-operated to remedy this situation. In fact, the more the federal authorities are open to French-Canadian aspirations, the more this will help to uproot this ideological trend which, to some extent, is apt to give an inferiority complex to those who have the heart and the courage to serve their country in the House of Commons.
That is why I ask the minister who was kind enough to remain, what will be the reaction of the federal authorities toward the initiative called the Estates General.

Well, we, as federal members, do not want to go back almost two hundred years.

Mr. Speaker, one week ago today, on Monday, June 19, as reported in Hansard at page 1657, I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) when we might expect the regulations under the Canada Labour (Safety) Code to be proclaimed and the provisions of that act to be put into effect. I found it shocking to hear the minister reply that it would be the end of the year before we could count on these steps being taken. As a result I posted this question for a late show.
I notice that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour is here to give the reply. I know that my hon. friend, the parliamentary secretary, is a man of many words, especially when his case is weak; but I want him to realize tonight that there is only one satisfactory answer to this question and that is that the timetable with respect to this matter will be stepped up.
The Canada Labour (Safety) Code, which is now on the statute books, was read for the first time in this house in July, 1966. It had been put through all stages, passed by both houses and given royal assent by December 21, 1966. The parliament secretary will recall that when we dealt with this matter in the House of Commons committee on labour and employment we were urged by the government to expedite the passage of this legislation. Members of the committee felt that two or three minor amendments should be made but we were persuaded by the minister and those associated with him not to press for these amendments because it would mean that the bill would have to return to the Senate, and that would cause delay. We were told that there was great desire and anxiety to put this legislation into effect, and that this would be done as soon as we passed it.
I remind the parliamentary secretary that this matter has been kicking around for a long time; it was around before this government came to power; it was around during the regime of the previous government which had a bill not unlike the one which was


finally passed. In other words, the Department of Labour has been working on this matter for a long time.
To be told therefore six months after the legislation has been passed that it will take another six months to bring it into effect is simply not good enough-especially when one realizes that the department's record with regard to the companion piece of legislation, the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, leaves much to be desired in terms of the many instances where the provisions of that act are not being enforced. It is not encouraging now to be told that the legislation being considered in this question will not be in effect for another six months.
The result is that those in railway shops and other places coming under federal labour jurisdiction, where there is no inspection on health or safety matters, because the provinces cannot come in and because the federal government has not entered the field, are wondering what is to happen and when something is to be done.
I said that this matter has been around for several years and dates back to the regime of the previous government. As the parliamentary secretary knows, the whole problem has been of concern to the Department of Labour and other departments for many years, indeed for several decades. I plead with the government to cease giving excuses about federal-provincial arrangements, and to cease telling us that the legislation will be implemented one year after it has been passed. From experience I know that when the government says it will take one year from the time legislation is passed to put it into effect, it will probably take two years, but there is no excuse for that kind of delay.
The government has been aware of this problem for a long time. I urge that action be taken in order that the provisions of this desirable legislation may be put into effect, so that employees in shops and factories under federal labour jurisdiction can have the benefit of this health and safety legislation without further delay.

Strange as it may seem, our abundant water is the only natural resource we still control in Canada. Since the unfortunate signing of the Columbia river treaty there has been a great awakening of interest right across Canada in the question of our water reserves on the part of professional persons, conservation groups, trade unions, municipal councils and groups of various types, including the provincial governments and, finally, the federal government.
This is the one advantage we have gained from the signing of the Columbia river treaty-it has alerted Canadians to the situation which exists with respect to our water resources. There is a growing concern about the supply of our water resources and their ability to meet the needs of future generations.
On this account there has been a growing demand for a national water policy. We cannot have a national water policy until we 27053-126
